html:
SMTO-AUT-0025 — This Google sign-in link is no longer valid

GUID: cf2d7c9d-c925-5828-9577-ee4874c26aa7
Slug: google-oauth-state-invalid
Domain: AUT · Subsystem: google-workspace

What happened

  • Google sent you back to SMTO, but the reply didn't match a current sign-in request. The link may have been old or already used, SMTO may have restarted, or its Google app setup changed. Nothing was saved.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Close any old Google sign-in tabs, and don't reuse sign-in links from earlier messages or bookmarks. Each link works only once, and only for the sign-in request that created it.
  2. Ask SMTO to connect your Google account again, then open the new link and finish within 10 minutes, signing in with the Google account you intend to use. A fresh link creates a new sign-in request that SMTO is actually waiting for.
  3. Don't restart SMTO or edit the Google app entry in Parameter Store until the sign-in page says you're connected. SMTO forgets unfinished sign-ins when it restarts and rejects them if the Google app setup changes meanwhile.
  4. If the sign-in page keeps showing Authorization failed or expired, ask the person who manages SMTO to check that SMTO's web address matches the return address in the Google app entry. Google must send you back to the same SMTO address the sign-in expects, or SMTO can't match the reply.

What success looks like

  • The Google sign-in tab says your email is connected and you can close the window.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send it to the person who manages SMTO. Don't copy sign-in links or codes from the browser's address bar into the conversation.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Google browser authorization rejected the callback because of missing, unknown or already used state, a redirect URI mismatch, duplicate callback parameters, or a changed Google app revision.

What this means

  • Shared browser authorization rejects missing/reused state, callback mismatch, duplicate callback fields or a changed application revision. Authorization establishes a particular connection, account and scope. It neither expands operation permissions nor proves the outcome of a request already dispatched.

Why this can happen

  • Shared browser authorization rejects missing/reused state, callback mismatch, duplicate callback fields or a changed application revision.

How to diagnose it

  • Compare the pending request and registered callback; restart after an application change rather than reusing the response.

How to fix it

  • Start a new auth.google_connect consent: pending state is single-use, held only in server memory for 10 minutes, and lost on restart. If it recurs, confirm the callback reaches exactly the pending redirect_uri (for web clients the registered /api/agent/google/oauth/callback URL, including behind any proxy), that nothing duplicates the code, state or error query parameters, and that the google_oauth_app record is not modified between start and callback.
  • Restart auth.google_connect. OAuth callbacks are single-use and bound to the original application revision.

Retry and execution caution

  • Confirm account identity and required features before retrying.

How to verify the fix

  • A fresh single-use callback matches the unchanged pending Google application and request.

What not to do

  • Do not expose client secrets, tokens, codes or PKCE verifiers.
  • Do not switch accounts or repeat uncertain mutations automatically.

Technical notes

  • Authorization establishes a particular connection, account and scope. It neither expands operation permissions nor proves the outcome of a request already dispatched.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
